chapter_theme: The pallor of longing (பசலை), the woman's most visible symptom, personified as a creature that rides her body, moves in the instant he moves away, and earns her the town's blame while he escapes it. She ends by offering her body as the price of his good name.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her first alone (1181), then answering her friend: on why it came (1182-1187), and then with growing irritation at the friend's blame of her and of him (1188-1190).

1181.reading: The woman, to herself, asks to whom she can describe her pallor, since she herself agreed to the absence of the man who loves her.
1181.nuance: Consent has closed off complaint. Parimelazhagar reads every word of this as her logic: having agreed, she feels it would be a further wrong even to tell anyone. 1181 is the first verse of the chapter, so the book's most visible symptom starts with her taking responsibility for it.

1182.reading: The woman says the pallor climbs on and rides over her body, proud that he is the one who gave it.
1182.nuance: Parimelazhagar uses the chariot-and-rider sense of இவர்தல் and adds that this is a claim of right, like a retainer's, which she can't resist because it comes from him. By his reading she is also comforting her friend: it's riding me by right, so don't worry. For Manakkudavar, she is saying that it isn't her doing, so take it up with him.

1183.reading: The woman says he took away her grace and modesty, and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange.
1183.nuance: The language is commercial: கைம்மாறா, 'in exchange'. Parimelazhagar notices the crossed pairing, in which sickness replaces modesty, since the more she tries to suppress it, the more it grows, and pallor replaces grace. He takes சாயல் as bodily beauty, and Manakkudavar as femininity (பெண்மை).

1184.reading: The woman says she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits, and still the pallor comes, a kind of cheating.
1184.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this a small argument: body follows mind and speech, and both are faithfully his, so the body shouldn't have paled. The verse never accuses her of faithlessness; the pallor is the deceiver.

1185.reading: The woman says: look there, her lover is going, and look here, the pallor is spreading over her body.
1185.nuance: The verse is built only from the pointing words உவக்காண் and இவக்காண், which turn distance into simultaneity. Parimelazhagar compares his leaving and the pallor's coming to the changing of day and night. He treats it as a memory of a past parting, and Manakkudavar as happening right now.

1186.reading: The woman says pallor watches for her lover's embrace to weaken, as darkness watches for a lamp to falter.
1186.nuance: Darkness isn't an enemy that attacks; it is simply what is there when the lamp fails. Read so, pallor is her natural state, and his embrace is what holds it off. Parimelazhagar's conclusion: if it waits for this tiny opening, what won't it do in a real separation?

1187.reading: The woman says she lay in his embrace and turned slightly, and at that the pallor was on her so thick it could be scooped up.
1187.nuance: This is the chapter's most vivid hyperbole, and it is almost comic in its domesticity. Manakkudavar's setting makes it sad: he has left without telling her, and the friend sees the change in her next morning and is told this.

1188.reading: The woman says people will say she has grown pale, and no one says he has left her.
1188.nuance: A flat remark about how blame is apportioned. The cause is invisible and the symptom is on her skin, so she bears the talk. Parimelazhagar reads the plural 'people' as aimed at the friend, whom she refuses to name in her anger.

1189.reading: The woman says let her body go pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is in a good state.

positions.position: நன்னிலையர் means blameless in the friend's eyes: since he must be held faultless, what does her body matter? This is bitter.
positions.quote: முன் இப்பிரிவின் கொடுமையறியாத என்னை இதற்கு உடம்படுத்திப் பிரிந்தவர் தவறிலராகவே வேண்டுவது

positions.position: The condition means he should suffer as she does, which is close to a curse.
positions.quote: நம்மைக் காதலித்த வரும் நம்மைப் போலத் துன்பமுறுவராயின்

positions.position: It means if he is well, and so it is a loving sacrifice.

1190.reading: The woman says that being called pale is good, if they won't spread talk of how unkind the man who won her has been.
1190.nuance: Parimelazhagar pushes பசப்பெனப் பேர் to its limit: not 'she has pallor' but 'she is pallor', a loss of identity she says she will welcome. He also says she speaks in scorn at the friend, who has criticised him to help her. Her good name is what she is ready to give for his.

links.note: 1130 insists he lives in her heart, so he has not gone anywhere. In 1184 her mind and words are full of him, but her skin has its own view. Her body undercuts what chapter 113 argues.

Both are inventories. The man in 1133 once had shame and manliness, and now has the palmyra horse, an instrument he can use. The woman in 1183 had grace and shame, and has been left sickness and pallor. Only his new possession is a tool.
In 1149 he has left her and the talk is about her; she can't be ashamed. In 1188 she states the injustice directly: the talk notices the symptom and not who caused it.

source_issues: 1187-1188: Parimelazhagar's commentary on 1188 is merged into his 1187 entry, including the verse text, while 1188 shows no aligned Parimelazhagar. The 1188 commentary was read and summarised in the nuance, but can't be quoted under the check.
1188: Manakkudavar also has no aligned commentary.
1182: Pope's entry places his prose inside the couplet field with a stray '< br>', leaving the prose field empty.
1184: Pope's prose is cut off mid-sentence ('and this is').
1190: Parimelazhagar's headnote has தரைமகள், a typo for தலைமகள்.
